full.text: The human heart
The heart has four chambers: two atria and two ventricles. The right side pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs; the left side pumps oxygenated blood to the body (double circulation).

items: Atrioventricular valves (tricuspid and bicuspid) stop backflow into the atria
Semilunar valves stop backflow from the arteries into the ventricles
The left ventricle wall is thickest because it pumps blood around the whole body

full.text: Cardiac cycle
Atrial systole, ventricular systole and diastole. The heartbeat starts at the sinoatrial node (pacemaker), spreads to the atrioventricular node, then down the bundle of His and Purkinje fibres.
The heartbeat starts in the heart muscle itself, without nervous stimulation.
Blood vessels

items: Arteries: thick muscular, elastic walls; high pressure
Veins: thin walls, wide lumen, valves; low pressure
Capillaries: one cell thick, for exchange

AV valves and semilunar valves prevent backflow
SAN, AVN, bundle of His, Purkinje fibres

full.text: The human kidney
The functional unit of the kidney is the nephron.

items: Ultrafiltration in the glomerulus and Bowman's capsule: small molecules pass out under high pressure
Selective reabsorption in the proximal convoluted tubule: all glucose, amino acids and much water and salts return to the blood
Loop of Henle: creates a high salt concentration in the medulla
Distal tubule and collecting duct: water reabsorption controlled by *ADH*

full.text: Filtration of blood under high pressure through the glomerular capillary walls and basement membrane, leaving cells and large proteins behind.
Osmoregulation

When blood water potential falls, the hypothalamus detects it and the posterior pituitary releases ADH. ADH makes the collecting duct more permeable to water, so more water is reabsorbed and urine becomes concentrated.

full.title: Past-paper tip
full.text: Glucose in urine is a sign that blood glucose is above the kidney's reabsorption threshold, as in diabetes mellitus.

items: Nephron = functional unit
Glomerulus + Bowman's capsule: ultrafiltration
PCT: reabsorbs glucose, amino acids, water
Loop of Henle: salty medulla
Collecting duct: water reabsorption under ADH
ADH from posterior pituitary

full.text: The neuron
A neuron has a cell body, dendrites that receive impulses and an axon that carries them away. Many axons have a myelin sheath with gaps called nodes of Ranvier.
The potential difference of about -70 mV across the membrane of a neuron that is not conducting an impulse.
Action potential

items: Depolarisation: sodium channels open and Na+ ions enter
Repolarisation: potassium channels open and K+ ions leave
The sodium-potassium pump restores the resting potential

full.text: In myelinated axons the impulse jumps from node to node (saltatory conduction), which is faster.
Synapse
At a synapse the impulse causes release of a neurotransmitter such as acetylcholine, which diffuses across the cleft and binds to receptors on the next neuron.

full.title: Past-paper tip
full.text: Synapses make transmission one-way because neurotransmitter is released only from the presynaptic side.

items: Dendrites in, axon out, myelin speeds conduction
Resting potential about -70 mV
Depolarisation: Na+ in; repolarisation: K+ out
Saltatory conduction between nodes of Ranvier
Synapse: neurotransmitter crosses the cleft; one-way

written.stem: Explain how the heartbeat is started and coordinated.
written.model_answer: The heartbeat is myogenic. The sinoatrial node sends a wave of excitation over the atria, which contract. The atrioventricular node delays it, then passes it down the bundle of His and Purkinje fibres so the ventricles contract from the apex upwards.

points.text: Myogenic / SA node is the pacemaker
Bundle of His / Purkinje fibres, ventricles contract

written.stem: Describe how urine is formed in a nephron.
written.model_answer: Blood is filtered under high pressure in the glomerulus into Bowman's capsule (ultrafiltration). Glucose, amino acids, salts and water are selectively reabsorbed in the proximal tubule. The loop of Henle concentrates salts in the medulla. Water is reabsorbed from the collecting duct under the control of ADH.

points.text: Collecting duct water reabsorption with ADH

written.stem: Explain how an action potential is produced in a neuron.
written.model_answer: A stimulus opens sodium channels, Na+ ions enter and the membrane depolarises. Then sodium channels close and potassium channels open, K+ ions leave and the membrane repolarises. The sodium-potassium pump restores the resting potential.

written.stem: Distinguish between active and passive immunity with one example of each.
written.model_answer: Active immunity is when the body makes its own antibodies and memory cells, for example after infection or vaccination; it is long-lasting. Passive immunity is when ready-made antibodies are received, for example from the mother or an antiserum; it is short-lived.

points.text: Active: body makes own antibodies / memory cells
Passive example: from mother / antiserum, short-lived

written.stem: Explain how blood glucose concentration is kept constant in humans.
written.model_answer: Blood glucose is detected by the islets of Langerhans in the pancreas. When it rises, beta cells secrete insulin, which increases uptake of glucose by cells and its conversion to glycogen in the liver and muscles, lowering blood glucose. When it falls, alpha cells secrete glucagon, which causes the liver to break down glycogen to glucose and raises blood glucose. This is negative feedback.

points.text: Insulin from beta cells lowers glucose
Glucagon from alpha cells raises glucose

written.stem: Describe the mechanism of breathing in humans.
written.model_answer: During inspiration the external intercostal muscles contract, moving the ribs up and out, and the diaphragm contracts and flattens. The thoracic volume increases and pressure falls below atmospheric, so air enters. During expiration these muscles relax, volume decreases, pressure rises above atmospheric and air is pushed out; in forced expiration the internal intercostals and abdominal muscles contract.

points.text: Intercostal muscles move ribs up and out
Volume increases, pressure decreases, air in
Expiration: muscles relax, air pushed out
Forced expiration: internal intercostals / abdominal muscles

ask.question: How does the kidney form urine?
ask.answer: In each nephron blood is filtered under pressure in the glomerulus into Bowman's capsule. Useful substances such as glucose and much water are reabsorbed in the proximal tubule. The loop of Henle and the collecting duct, controlled by ADH, adjust how much water is kept, and the rest leaves as urine.

sources.title: A/L Biology syllabus (2025), topic 5.11: The human kidney

ask.question: Why is the left ventricle wall thicker than the right?
ask.answer: The left ventricle pumps blood all around the body, which needs much higher pressure. The right ventricle pumps only to the nearby lungs, so it has a thinner muscular wall.

sources.title: A/L Biology syllabus (2025), topic 5.5: The human heart and blood vessels

ask.question: What is saltatory conduction?
ask.answer: In myelinated axons the action potential jumps from one node of Ranvier to the next, because the myelin sheath insulates the axon in between. This is saltatory conduction and makes the impulse much faster.

sources.title: A/L Biology syllabus (2025), topic 5.12: Nervous coordination and the neuron

ask.question: How do vaccines work?
ask.answer: A vaccine contains antigens from a weakened, killed or partial pathogen. The immune system makes antibodies and memory cells against it, so a later infection is met with a faster and stronger response. This is artificial active immunity.

ask.question: What does insulin do?
ask.answer: Insulin is secreted by the beta cells of the pancreas when blood glucose is high. It increases glucose uptake by cells and its conversion to glycogen in the liver and muscles, lowering blood glucose.
